item.title: Fiber-optic sensing unearths surprising complexity in small California earthquake
item.description: More than 20,000 earthquakes are located worldwide each year, but the vast majority of those are small—many too small to be felt by humans. Scientists have historically assumed most of these small earthquakes break as small, circular ruptures in which the rocks in a fault slip past each other in a single, smooth motion, and the crack spreads outward from one point like a ripple in a pond, unlike the behavior of most major earthquakes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why a warmer atmosphere doesn't guarantee more water in rivers
item.description: Austria experienced an exceptional drought in 2026. From the start of the year until the end of October, rainfall was around a third lower than the long-term average. The consequences are low river flows and groundwater levels. But how is water availability linked to global warming? Shouldn't a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more water vapor, also lead to more rainfall? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The world is experiencing a string of abnormally hot days—and records are being shattered
item.description: We're becoming used to seeing records being broken whenever we look at data telling us about Earth's climate. item.title: The US army just detonated a poison bomb over Iowa | Steven Donziger
item.description: The shocking situation in Iowa is a metaphor for much of what is wrong with the United States There’s no way to hide it: the US government just deliberately detonated a poison bomb of lead azide over the state of Iowa when a totally safe alternative was available. The problem in Iowa was relatively simple to solve. The army for decades had stored lead underground at a munitions facility. As far back as 2009, the government knew the lead was deteriorating and might blow up on its own. But it procrastinated. Finally, in March, the army hired a Georgia-based company to use a chemical spray to… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: As families gather for Thanksgiving, college science students need training to talk across societal divides
item.description: Most Americans have seen it happen. Relatives argue online about whether vaccines are safe and effective. Friends and neighbors trade jabs over climate change and whether anything should be done about it. Public officials and scientists disagree, loudly, about what causes autism or which vaccines children should get and when. No one gives an inch, and the rifts rarely heal. This Thanksgiving, after a contentious election season, many of those conversations will happen face to face around the dinner table. Fuente: Phys.org.
